pass_a_gloss: [...] is of the one who sent me: That everything which he has given me I may not lose of it, but I will raise it on the last day. So for achieving life for those who believe in him, he did not make insults, not scourges, not the trial of spittings a thing to be rejected, although being God by nature and true Lord. Then he says as man: And the Lord became my helper, because of this I was not turned back, but I set my face like solid rock, and I knew that I will surely not be shamed, because the one who justified me draws near. He speaks then humanly, as I said, and in no way unlike the measures of the emptying. But he seems to hint through these words the penalty that fell upon those words because of the impiety toward him. For the Lord, he says, became my helper. Similar as if he should say: I having given my back to scourges, and my cheeks to blows, and having suffered also the sufferings upon the cross, the Father became helper. For he defended, and did not allow his own Son to be wholly turned back, nor yet to be put to shame. For they have been punished, and have paid penalties of the offences against me, those who dared to fight God. And having added that, The one who justified me draws near, he hinted again elegantly that not after long nor into postponement will the things of the penalty run upon those who acted drunkenly outrageous toward him, but as it were near, and at the foot of the attempts it will walk. And we say the Son was justified in some such manner. For since, being righteous, and in no way as having become liable to faults, they dared to kill [him], they have been punished, just as I said, and the punishment of those who suffered has borne witness to the wholly blameless [state] of the one insulted unholily by them. The God and Father said something such: And I will give the wicked in return for his burial, and the rich in return for his death. And rich and wicked he names the leaders of the Jews. For being sick with extreme love of money, they were carried down through it into the wickedness against him. For although having recognized him they were saying: This is the heir; come, let us kill, and have for ourselves his inheritance. [Lemma, Isaiah 50:8:] Who is the one judged with me? Let him stand against together. Who is the one judged with me? Let him draw near to me. That being righteous and wholly innocent, for he did not do sins, he endured the drunken outrages from the Jews, the divine prophet himself also will confirm, saying about him: See how the righteous perished, and no one receives it to heart. And again as from the person of the Jews about him: Let us bind the righteous one, because he is troublesome to us. And the thing itself would shout it through. For the divine and pure nature of the Word [the section breaks off].
pass_b_english: … is the will of him who sent me, “that of all that he has given me I should lose nothing, but raise it up on the last day” (John 6:39). So, to win life for those who believe in him, he did not refuse insults, or whips, or the trial of being spat upon, though he is God by nature and true Lord.

Then he says, as a man: “And the Lord became my helper; therefore I was not put to shame, but I set my face like a solid rock, and I knew that I would not be ashamed, because he who justifies me draws near” (Isaiah 50:7-8). So he speaks in a human way, as I said, and in no way out of keeping with the measures of his self-emptying.

Yet through these words he seems to hint at the judgment that came down on them for their impiety toward him. For he says, “The Lord became my helper.” It is as if he said: When I had given my back to whips and my cheeks to blows (Isaiah 50:6), and had suffered the sufferings on the cross as well, the Father became my helper. For he came to his defense, and did not allow his own Son to be utterly disgraced, nor indeed to be put to shame. For those who dared to fight against God have been punished, and have paid the penalty for their offenses against me.

By adding, “He who justifies me draws near,” he again deftly made plain that the judgment on those who had outraged him would not be far off or put off, but would come near, as it were, and follow close on the heels of their deeds.

We say that the Son was justified in this way. Since they dared to kill him, though he was righteous and in no way guilty of any fault, they have been punished, as I said; and the punishment of those who suffered it has borne witness that he whom they so impiously outraged was wholly blameless. God the Father said something of this kind: “And I will give the wicked in return for his burial, and the rich in return for his death” (Isaiah 53:9).

By the rich and wicked he means the leaders of the Jews. For they were sick with an extreme love of money, and through it they were carried away into their wickedness against him. Indeed, although they had recognized him, they kept saying, “This is the heir; come, let us kill him and have his inheritance for ourselves” (Matthew 21:38).
“Who is the one who contends with me? Let him stand up against me together. Who is the one who contends with me? Let him come near to me” (Isaiah 50:8).

That he was righteous and wholly innocent (for he committed no sin; 1 Peter 2:22), and yet endured the drunken outrages of the Jews, the divine prophet himself will confirm when he says of him, “See how the righteous one has perished, and no one takes it to heart” (Isaiah 57:1); and again, as in the person of the Jews, speaking of him: “Let us bind the righteous one, for he is troublesome to us” (Isaiah 3:10). The fact itself would proclaim it aloud. For the divine and pure nature of the Word …

choices.english: We say that the Son was justified in this way
choices.why: Cyril explains: the punishment of his killers bore witness that he was blameless.
Cyril's reading of 'the rich' of Isaiah 53:9 as the Jewish leaders.

choices.why: Septuagint Isaiah 3:10; the Hebrew reads differently.
